The rapid expansion of biomedical literature has created substantial challenges in retrieving and synthesizing relevant knowledge, particularly for novice and interdisciplinary users. Conventional keyword-based methods often lack semantic depth, whereas traditional topic modelling techniques struggle to capture domain-specific contexts and rarely integrate structured metadata, such as medical subject headings (MeSH). To address these limitations, this study introduces a dual-stream embedding framework that integrates unstructured textual content with curated biomedical metadata using transformer-based encoders and a parameterized fusion mechanism. The architecture combines contextual semantics from article titles and abstracts with expert-annotated MeSH descriptors and incorporates a large language model to generate concise and human-readable topic labels. Experimental results show that three of the four evaluated embedding configurations outperformed the single-stream baseline and that the dual-stream fusion surpassed all ablation models built from the same inputs. The best configuration, Dual PubMedBERT, achieved the highest overall topic modelling quality, improving the combined measure of topic coherence and topic diversity by 7.3% relative to the baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual textual embeddings with structured biomedical metadata using the proposed fusion mechanism. This approach is scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable, providing both a methodological advancement in semantic topic modelling and a practical foundation for the development of biomedical information retrieval systems, semantic search engines, and thematic exploration tools across knowledge-intensive domains.

European transport and logistics sectors are undergoing a transformative shift driven by the increasing adoption of data-driven solutions. This paper explores challenges and opportunities associated with implementing data-sharing frameworks and interoperable systems, drawing insights from European initiatives such as KEYSTONE and HOLOGISTICS projects and DTLF group. Fragmented data ecosystems and associated sociotechnical barriers, such as lack of inter-organisational trust and concerns over data sovereignty, significant barriers to realising the full potential of data-driven transport. However, innovations like federated platforms, real-time data utilisation and collaborative frameworks have demonstrated their ability to enhance operational efficiency, reduce environmental impact and improve resilience across multimodal transport networks. This paper presents valuable lessons learned, highlighting practical outcomes, including reduced times, optimised resource allocation, and emissions reductions. It also offers policy recommendations and a technological roadmap to address remaining barriers, scale solutions, and align with European Union’s strategic objectives for sustainability and digital integration, particularly in support of EU’s Green Deal and climate neutrality targets for 2050, also in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. By addressing these challenges and leveraging emerging technologies, Europe’s transport and logistics sectors can achieve cleaner, more resilient, and connected mobility systems, setting a global benchmark for sustainable innovation.

Bladder cancer is among the most recurrence-prone malignancies, and its management remains anchored to invasive cystoscopy and cytology, which have limited sensitivity. Urine, which is in direct contact with the tumor, carries a rich molecular cargo, including urinary tumor-derived DNA (utDNA), the tumor-derived fraction of urinary cell-free DNA, alongside methylation marks, extracellular vesicle (EV) cargo, and exfoliated cells. These components can now be interrogated through multi-omics profiling and interpreted using artificial intelligence (AI). In this Mini Review, we integrate these layers into a single translational framework: microfluidic “urine-on-chip” technologies convert a drop of urine into standardized, analysis-ready multi-omic data, while machine learning and deep learning models—increasingly governed by STARD-AI/TRIPOD + AI reporting standards—transform these data into diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment-response predictions. We highlight clinically mature anchors, including the utMeMA methylation assay (90.0%/83.1%), the Uromonitor mutation test (TERT/FGFR3/KRAS; 80.2%/96.9%, meta-analysis), chip-based cytometry for detecting high-grade disease, and an externally validated autonomous urine cytology system. These figures are assay-specific and should not be interpreted as platform-wide benchmarks. Finally, we define the priorities—pre-analytical standardization, external validation, and cost-effectiveness—that will advance urinary multi-omic AI from its current performance level into routine practice along a “detect–decide–treat–monitor” digital management pathway.

Metro operators worldwide face critical fail-to-board events at centralised interchange stations, where local mitigation (e.g., schedule adjustments or empty-train insertion) can displace congestion downstream. We propose a calibrated digital twin of the Panama Metro integrated with two AI optimisation methods: a genetic algorithm and a deep reinforcement learning agent. Using real operational data from morning peak hours, the framework evaluates dispatching policies to minimise network-wide fail-to-board and is benchmarked against manual control and a commercial solver with station-level targets. The commercial solver reduced fail-to-board at Central Station by 37% but required 8–18 min per optimisation. The genetic algorithm achieved comparable reduction (33%) in 60–120 s while optimising network-wide performance. Deep reinforcement learning reached similar performance (32%) with $$\sim $$ ∼ 1 s inference, enabling near-real-time deployment in metro control rooms. Unlike station-level optimisation, network-wide optimisation prevents congestion displacement to upstream stations, resulting in lower spillover while maintaining similar fail-to-board reduction across the entire network.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can suggest wording, explain language, and increasingly contribute to feedback and assessment. The central issue is not only what these systems generate, but when learners, teachers, and institutions begin to treat their outputs as reasons for judging language. Existing research addresses language ideology, distributed agency, algorithmic normativity, trust, assessment, and AI governance, but these literatures use different concepts for influence, authority, and institutional power. This article develops a multilevel framework of linguistic authority escalation through a critical integrative review focused primarily on English-dominant higher-education writing and assessment. In the framework, authority in the strict sense refers to attributed epistemic or normative standing; operational uptake is causal influence, and regulatory consequentiality is institutional power. The framework differentiates the initiator, subject, decision-maker, and accountable actor, and represents the source of authorisation, the subject’s degree of meaningful choice, and the durability of system embedding as co-occurring configurational conditions rather than alternative routes. It also distinguishes epistemic warrant, procedural legitimacy, substantive linguistic justice, and assessment validity as different standards for evaluating AI-mediated judgement. A literature-grounded worked case shows how the same model suggestion can remain optional assistance or acquire institutional force depending on these relations. The framework helps educational linguists identify when GenAI support preserves evaluative control and when opaque linguistic norms become difficult to contest, directing pedagogy and governance towards norm-explicit feedback, meaningful alternatives, task-specific evidence, appeal, and clear answerability.

Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.

documents.abstract: Simulators play a crucial role in the aerospace industry, ranging from simple desktop models to advanced Level D simulators used for pilot training. While most non-gaming simulators focus on crew training and client illustration, there is a notable deficiency in simulators that assist with cockpit design. Current methods primarily utilize standard CAD/CAE software alongside Digital Human Models, which often lack adequate functionality for comprehensive human factor evaluation for design optimization. This paper introduces a configurable Virtual Reality Spacecraft Simulator that is calibrated with data from microgravity studies from the International Space Station collected from two astronauts. The VR simulator is also integrated with human factor evaluation suit like eye gaze and EEG trackers. The proposed VR simulator implements immersive task execution in scenarios such as deorbiting manoeuvres, emergency responses, and robotic arm operations, while also comparing task completion times in microgravity conditions. Three applications of the VR spacecraft simulator are presented to highlight prospectives uses for informed design decisions.

Industries often hold valuable data locked in silos, limiting both the amount and diversity of data available for training machine learning models and consequently reducing accuracy and generalization capabilities. Centralizing sensitive data or sharing it with third parties introduces significant privacy and security risks, complicating data governance and control. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these challenges by enabling collaborative model training without the need to transfer raw data, thus preserving privacy while harnessing distributed information. Complementarily, Data Spaces provide a secure framework for trusted data exchange through standardized protocols and robust governance, ensuring interoperability and responsible data use. By integrating FL within a Data Space, organizations can overcome the dual hurdles of data silos and stringent privacy requirements, while FL inherently safeguards privacy by enabling collaborative model training without raw data transfer, its integration within a Data Space offers enhanced security and governance beyond traditional FL. This approach ensures that all interactions, from service discovery to model exchange, are governed by explicit policies and contracts, providing unprecedented traceability and control over the collaborative AI lifecycle. This paper presents a novel architecture implemented within the Mondragon-X Industrial Data Space that seamlessly embeds the FL workflow. Leveraging advanced EDC connectors, dedicated APIs, and the Flower AI framework in a hybrid edge-cloud environment, our approach enables continuous model updates, collaborative improvements, and strict data sovereignty, thereby establishing a scalable foundation for developing powerful and privacy-preserving industrial artificial intelligence (AI) solutions.

documents.abstract: Manufacturing is quickly moving toward a human-centered approach, adjusting production systems to match workers’ needs, preferences, skills, and mental or physical state. Even though Human Factors are important in collaborative robotics, there’s little research on how they affect AI-based manufacturing. This gap highlights the need for new Knowledge Engineering solutions that represent in a formal and structured way also human-centric attributes within manufacturing environments. In this paper, we propose the extension of a state of the art ontology for human-robot collaboration by, first, identifying which HF are most relevant to collaborative manufacturing and, then, defining how they can be effectively represented. Including HF into knowledge representation enables AI-based robot control to consider worker conditions and dynamically adapt their task execution accordingly ensuring both safety, efficiency and worker well-being.

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) is one of the most studied probiotic strains, with an immunological fingerprint that has evolved over three decades of research. The exponential growth of biomedical literature has created a scalability crisis exceeding human synthesis capacity. This study aimed to elucidate LGG’s immunomodulatory role using a zero-cost, high-speed, hybrid human-AI workflow, leveraging free Model-platform systems as a scalable screening tool accessible to any researcher regardless of institutional affiliation. An operative pipeline based on four specialized prompts was developed to interrogate three Model-platform systems architectures (Gemini 3 Flash, Perplexity Academic, and Claude Sonnet 4.6), screening 37 years of PubMed literature (1989–2026). Performance was benchmarked against a human-validated Gold Standard using Sensitivity, Specificity, and Spearman Correlation, with a “Semantic Floor” analysis investigating False Negatives. A paradigm shift emerged: historical studies (pre-2019) focused on mucosal barrier integrity and IgA production, while recent research (2019–2026) emphasizes complex molecular signaling (IL-22, Type-I Interferons, Inflammasome modulation). A consistent core fingerprint persisted, characterized by TNF-α/IL-6 suppression and IL-10 upregulation, while IFNg showed context-dependent dual modulation. Gemini 3 Flash showed superior sensitivity (0.93–0.97), while Perplexity Academic achieved near-perfect specificity (0.99) due to its Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture which mitigated hallucinations. The Spearman Heatmap revealed a correlation coefficient near zero between Gemini and Perplexity sessions, reflecting their divergent scoring dynamics. LGG research has shifted from mucosal barrier protection to complex molecular signaling. Synergy between different model-platform systems architectures allows researchers to act as AI-orchestrators, focusing on critical interpretation rather than mechanical extraction. Established knowledge on this subject. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) is one of the most studied probiotic strains, with a well-documented immunomodulatory profile. Biomedical literature is growing exponentially and model-platform systems are emerging as tools for accelerating evidence synthesis, but their reliability and complementarity in biomedical research remain poorly characterized. Significant and/or new findings of this study. We validated a zero-cost, hybrid human-AI pipeline using three distinct model-platform systems architectures to screen 37 years of PubMed literature on LGG. We identified a shift in LGG research, from mucosal barrier/IgA focus to a more recent interest in complex molecular signaling (IL-22, Type I IFN, inflammasome). A consistent core immunological fingerprint (TNF-α/IL-6 suppression, IL-10/IFN-γ upregulation) persisted across three decades. We defined a "Semantic Floor," including a novel "Title Trap" phenomenon, highlighting key limitations requiring human oversight in AI-assisted synthesis.

Water quality is essential for environmental sustainability and public health, yet conventional laboratory-based monitoring is costly and slow. Machine learning (ML) has been proposed as an alternative, but algorithm performance is inconsistent across studies and seldom compared on identical target parameters. This study synthesizes ML algorithm use and performance in predicting water quality parameters. A structured narrative literature review searched Scopus for English-language publications from 2015 to 2026 using keywords combining machine learning, deep learning, or artificial intelligence with water quality and prediction, forecasting, or classification. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria; 37 publications were analyzed. Algorithms, target parameters, validation strategies, and metrics (R², RMSE, MAE) were extracted and synthesized narratively, with performance grouped by target parameter, not compared across targets. Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, neural networks, and boosting algorithms (XGBoost, AdaBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM) were most frequently used, while the Water Quality Index (WQI) was the most frequently predicted target, followed by dissolved oxygen (DO), pH, and biochemical oxygen demand (BOD). Ensemble and boosting models generally performed strongly; for example, XGBoost reached R² = 0.93 and RMSE = 0.047 for the Irrigation Water Quality Index, and an attention-based LSTM reached R² = 0.985 for daily DO. However, no algorithm was universally superior, and external validation remained rare. Algorithm selection should consider data characteristics, target parameter, evaluation metrics, and interpretability.

As artificial intelligence rapidly evolves from a subordinate tool into autonomous, agentic systems, it threatens to outgrow both traditional safety guardrails and existing legal frameworks. While current laws treat AI strictly as property devoid of legal personhood, structural loopholes such as memberless limited liability companies (LLCs) and algorithmically governed decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) theoretically enable AI to hijack corporate personhood to execute contracts, hold property, and wield protected free-speech rights without human intervention. Although centralized corporate oversight and the performance limits of independent open-weight models temporarily keep this risk contained, advancing decentralized computing is rapidly narrowing that buffer. Society therefore faces a window of opportunity to reform legal boundaries and close these corporate loopholes before autonomous AI transitions to an independent, legally shielded actor.

Quality control is a significant topic for manufacturing under the scope of industry 5.0, while industries are devoting more efforts for resilient and sustainable processes but also while keeping the human in the loop. Under this scope, different human-robot collaborative technologies have emerged in order to address issues affecting the quality of different products, processes or equipment involved in manufacturing scenarios. This paper presents a methodology towards the efficient artificial intelligence (AI )- driven quality control of applications involving the collaboration between robots and human operators. The proposed approach involves aspects related to both robots and humans, aiming to robustly adapt the factors responsible for the quality of the final product itself. An AI-based framework is also deployed implementing the proposed methodology under real conditions. The proposed methodology is being applied in an industrial scenario derived from the automotive sector, where the accurate assembly of high payload parts is required under human-robot collaborative applications.

Hengjie is a runtime quality-assurance mechanism for control software driven by external planners, including large language models (LLMs). Because planner output is untrusted, release is gated: the kernel releases a candidate only after robust predictive verification against state uncertainty and the committed queue, with a certified fallback. For the discrete-time model, every released action remains covered by the execution invariant under the premises, for any proposer. The characterisation is a pre-registered, frozen-protocol study of a simulated thermal process under bounded faults (424 executable cells, failures and counterexamples retained). The protected configurations (legacy B, 34 cells; B2, 88 cells) recorded 0 violation minutes and 0 uncovered-authorisation minutes; the unprotected configuration recorded 25,792 and 34,433, respectively. Under one-slot delay the protected paths stayed safe but completed 10–11 of 1,440 task minutes. A pre-registered budget study re-ran the reviewed LLM cells at 4× and 16× the frozen budget and cut fallback share from 0.964 to 0.507, but left the task ratio identical (0.9981; non-LLM configuration 0.9983): budget changed which controller holds the band, not the outcome. A control-barrier-function safety filter wrapping the same proposer, run as an exact replica in the same slots as a twelve-cell engineering baseline, recorded zero violation minutes and held the disconnection cells where the heuristic chain B collapsed. Decision latency: median 1.32–1.37 s per 60 s tick. All frozen-batch quantities were independently recomputed from a public replication package with zero discrepancies; reproducing a published predictive-safety baseline deviated by +31.4%, the cause undetermined after pre-registered single-factor diagnosis.

documents.abstract: Enterprises increasingly combine large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and autonomous software agents with existing enterprise architecture, knowledge management, and analytics investments, yet these capabilities are commonly adopted as isolated point solutions without a shared architectural foundation for organizational knowledge, decision reasoning, human accountability, or continuous assurance. This fragmentation leaves organizations unable to explain how an automated recommendation was produced, to bound what an autonomous agent may do, or to demonstrate governance to auditors, regulators, and boards. This paper asks how enterprise knowledge, decision support, agent execution, and governance can be structured as one coherent architecture. Using a literature-grounded conceptual synthesis across enterprise architecture, knowledge management, retrieval-augmented generation, decision intelligence, agentic artificial intelligence, and artificial intelligence governance, the paper derives a consolidated research gap and proposes the Governed Cognitive Enterprise Architecture: six integrated layers, a human accountability boundary, a structural formal representation, an operational lifecycle, and a maturity model, the Cognitive Enterprise Readiness Index, for organizational self-assessment. The architecture is evaluated conceptually against explicit criteria for completeness, capability integration, and governance alignment, and is compared with the reviewed literature through a source-referenced framework rather than an experimental benchmark. The principal contribution is an integrated architectural vocabulary and structure that treats human accountability and continuous assurance as first-class concerns alongside knowledge and decision capability. As a conceptual reference architecture it has not been empirically validated in an operational enterprise; expert evaluation, case-study, and quantitative validation are specified as future work.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background and Objective The misdiagnosis of epilepsy is a problem that 25-30% of patients all around the world have to deal with, which results in the use of incorrect treatments, imposing restrictions on life unnecessarily, and making other underlying conditions' care delayed. The limitations of the classic techniques are the subjectivity of EEG interpretation, 20-30% inter-observer variability, and ictal phenomena being only partially captured. This review evaluates thoroughly the potential of using artificial intelligence (AI) for detection of seizures and epilepsy management individually in order to tackle the diagnostic problems. Methodology: A detailed review of the literature has been done to consider the AI interventions in different areas, including deep learning-based EEG signal processing, computer vision for semiological characterization, new wearable biosensors, and machine learning methods to improve personalized treatment. The assessments of effectiveness focused on diagnostic accuracy, clinical validity, and the practicality of real-world implementation Results: AI offers a practical solution for addressing misdiagnosis and advancing precision medicine in epilepsy treatment. There is enough evidence to support the prompt use of validated AI technology in clinical settings. This can enhance diagnosis accuracy, help tailor treatments for individual patients, and ensure broad access to quality epilepsy care. The presence of enforceable regulations, demonstrated effectiveness in clinical trials, and the pressing need to improve the lives of those impacted by epilepsy all support a teamwork-based approach to incorporating AI into regular clinical practice for epilepsy care. Conclusions: AI marks a paradigm shift from misdiagnosis to precision medicine to maximize care for patients with epilepsy. There is evidence to support the immediate utilization of innovative AI technology developed to improve diagnostic accuracy, specify and optimize treatment for individuals with epilepsy, and disseminate high-quality expert care to all patients, regardless of geography. The convergence of regulatory approval, proof of utility, and synthesized clinical need compel us to adopt a systematic integration of AI into daily practice for epilepsy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Due to rapid urbanisation, increased energy demands and climate change, cities have evolved to be much more intelligent in managing their energy. This is where Artificial Intelligence (AI) comes into play with sustainable smart cities. AI can be used for many purposes including renewable energy forecasting, smart grid optimisation, demand side management and fault detection. This paper provides a structured review of the literature regarding AI and Machine Learning (ML) used in sustainable energy management within Smart Cities. Twenty-two sources (mainly from 2019 to 2026) were reviewed and split into five categories of Renewable Energy Forecasting, Smart Grid Optimisation, Smart Building and Demand Side Management, Explainable AI and Smart City Sustainability. From this literature, it can be seen that deep learning techniques such as Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Hybrid Convolutional Neural Network and Long Short Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) and Transformers are dominating in forecasting applications. Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Agent systems are also becoming more popular in real time grid control. Overall though, the literature found that there are many issues surrounding the research and this includes lack of interpretability, scalability, poor quality data and high environmental costs when training large AI models. This paper will outline research gaps, suggest a new conceptual framework around accuracy, interpretability and deployability and suggest future research areas for creating trustworthy, scalable and sustainable AI smart energy systems for Smart Cities.

Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its translation to solid tumors remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, poor tumor infiltration, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, and on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Here, we present a safety-constrained artificial intelligence framework for rational CAR-T design in solid tumors. The workflow integrates four linked stages: CD-antigen prioritization, safety-by-design CAR architecture mapping, constrained large language model (LLM)–assisted reasoning, and statistical feature-structure analysis. Curated CD-antigen functional annotations and tumor-associated expression descriptors were encoded into a multi-criteria scoring system that stratified targets into high-confidence, conditional, and unsafe classes. Across the analyzed CD-antigen space, 38% of markers were classified as high-confidence candidates, 34% as conditional targets requiring logic-gated or controllable architectures, and 28% as unsafe targets because of predicted off-tumor risk. External benchmark analysis using MSLN, HER2/ERBB2, EGFR/EGFRvIII, CEA/CEACAM5, GD2, B7-H3/CD276, and CD47 supported the framework’s ability to distinguish direct targets from safety-constrained or unsuitable candidates. An updated four-model LLM benchmark, including GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.5, Grok 4.5, and Claude Sonnet 5, showed convergence toward dual-antigen logic-gated, trafficking-enhanced, and armored CAR designs, while revealing model-dependent differences in safety awareness, traceability, and hallucination risk. Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol showed the strongest safety-oriented performance, whereas Grok 4.5 required greater expert oversight. Correlation and clustering analyses further identified redundant safety-liability features and candidate antigen combinations for logic-gated CAR design. This study provides a reproducible, human-in-the-loop decision-support framework for generating safety-aware CAR-T hypotheses. The framework is computational and hypothesis-generating and does not constitute experimental validation of CAR-T efficacy or safety.

The angular radius 𝛾 of the red ring of an optical glory, a set of concentric colored rings observed in clouds in the anti-solar direction, is used to estimate cloud drop characteristic diameter as 𝑑 = 𝜆/𝛾, where we take 𝜆 = 0.650 μm. A photograph of a glory taken with an iPhone 12 mini camera from a commercial airplane with 𝛾 ≈ 0.043 = 2.5° yields 𝑑 ≈ 0.650 μm/0.043 = 15 μm. Based on Mie scattering calculations, we show that despite occasional departures, this “diffraction” estimate is surprisingly robust and nearly independent of refractive index. We argue that photographs of optical glories taken from commercial aircraft constitute a potentially vast crowd-sourced database that could supplement, when coincident, more advanced ground-based, airborne, and spaceborne lidar and radar observations, with machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) applications.

People often feel an idea more strongly in their mother tongue, and they soften a hard message so that the listener is not hurt. This study asks whether chat-based large language models (LLMs) handle hard messages with the same care in English, Hindi and Marathi. Ten industry situations, such as a rejected build, a loan denial and the removal of an engineer from duty, were given to ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in the three languages. The 90 collected messages were scored with a concept-matched word list that has five harshness categories and four softening categories. The scores were Harshness H, Softening S and Net tone N = H − S, with content coverage and length as extra checks. Differences between models were large (Kendall’s W of 0.30 for N and 0.56 for S). Differences between languages were small and not significant after correction. Gemini wrote short messages with almost no softening (S = 0.06), whereas ChatGPT and Claude used courtesy, regret and offers of help. Gemini also left out more key facts in Marathi (82% coverage) than in English (94%). Each cell holds one response, the word list was built after reading the data, and no human rater was used, so the results are exploratory.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Auto drivers are an important component of the local transport system, providing short-distance mobility and last-mile connectivity in towns and cities. Despite their contribution, their livelihood is affected by irregular earnings, rising operating costs, long working hours, road and traffic conditions, occupational health risks and limited social protection. This study examines the socio-economic profile, working conditions and major occupational challenges of auto drivers in Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli District. The study covers 150 auto drivers in Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli District. Data are presented for all 150 respondents and analysed using frequency distribution and percentage analysis. Percentage analysis and frequency distributions are used to summarise the available information. The results indicate that most respondents are aged 30–40, work for 8–10 hours daily, own their vehicles and report daily earnings in the ₹500–₹1,000 category. Poor road conditions, joint pain, fatigue and work-related pressure emerge as important concerns. The study recommends improvements in road infrastructure, access to welfare and health services, affordable finance and occupational health awareness.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Natural language interaction and physical environment understanding are two core challenges for improving the autonomy of home service robots. This paper provides a systematic review of the evolution from traditional robotic methods to embodied intelligence enabled by large language models (LLMs), vision-language models (VLMs), and vision-language-action (VLA) models. For environmental understanding, we review the transition from geometric maps to semantic representations and behavioral navigation, emphasizing the roles of semantic SLAM, hierarchical scene representations, and VLMs. For natural language interaction, we analyze the limitations of rule-based approaches and the advances enabled by LLMs in task planning, reasoning, and code generation. Unlike previous surveys focusing separately on perception or language interaction, this review establishes a unified taxonomy and analyzes representative LLM/VLM/VLA-based robotic systems. We further discuss emerging trends toward multimodal reasoning, language-guided action generation, and adaptive embodied intelligence, while identifying key challenges in generalization, real-time deployment, safety, and interpretability. Finally, future directions toward reliable and adaptive embodied robotic systems are discussed.

documents.abstract: Keynote: II International Meeting of UNESCO Chairs in Open, Digital and Distance Education, "Transforming Higher Education: People-Centred Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence." Madrid, 18-19 November, 2026.Every educational technology proposes a pedagogy. Jupyter notebooks, for example, by weaving narrative with code, invited a way of teaching computing as storytelling and live exploration; because they are open source, they also encouraged the sharing of learning resources and became ubiquitous. Generative AI proposes a pedagogy too, and its default is troubling: shaped like conversation, in everyday use it reverts to an antiquated model of instruction, the delivery of answers. Students who use AI as an answer machine develop an illusion of competence: the feeling of understanding without its substance. In this talk, I return to first principles. With Piaget and Papert, learners construct knowledge; with Gordon Pask, understanding is demonstrated by explaining it back in conversation; with Andrea diSessa, literacy is a social infrastructure, not only an individual skill. Read together, they suggest that the question for AI in education is not whether students converse with machines, but who does the explaining. Drawing on my own failed classroom experiment with an AI tutor, and on the innovation that followed—a scalable oral assessment I call the conversational exam, which restores the learner’s voice—I will argue for using AI as an amplifier of human conversation, and for investing in educators as the designers of those conversations.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Building on prior studies that have documented the dehumanization of the users of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, that is, the tendency for observers to attribute less humanness to individuals who use AI than to those who do not, the present research examines whether and how different AI use purposes (i.e., accuracy- vs. efficiency-driven use) influence this effect. We conducted four preregistered studies (total N = 1,270) spanning diverse professional domains. We observed that accuracy-driven AI use negatively predicted the dehumanization of AI users, whereas efficiency-driven AI use positively predicted such dehumanization (Study 1). Furthermore, accuracy-driven AI users elicited less dehumanization than their efficiency-driven counterparts did, a pattern that proved robust across both intuitive assessments of dehumanization (Study 2) and deliberative ratings of humanness traits (Studies 3 and 4). However, both accuracy- and efficiency-driven AI users were significantly dehumanized compared with non-AI users (Study 4), demonstrating that while purpose matters, AI user dehumanization persists. These findings extend the literature on the social cost of AI and offer novel insights into how human–AI interaction shapes interpersonal dynamics .
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Background Older hospitalized patients often live with multiple chronic conditions and face an increased risk of mortality. However, advance care planning (ACP) remains underused in China. Understanding the barriers to and facilitators of ACP among older hospitalized patients may inform strategies to support its implementation. Methods Between May and December 2025, we conducted semi-structured interviews with patients aged over 80 years, caregivers, and healthcare professionals at a Tertiary hospital in a city in western China. Interviews explored participants’ understanding of ACP, discussions about ACP, factors influencing patients’ engagement in or avoidance of ACP, and perceived strategies and support needs for promoting ACP. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Results We conducted 35 interviews with 5 physicians, 10 nurses, 10 patients, and 10 caregivers. Two of the 10 patients (20%) had completed an advance directive(AD). Twelve of the 15 healthcare professionals (80%) reported receiving regular ACP training. Four themes that affect the implementation of ACP were identified (1)Awareness of ACP and sources of information; (2) Psychosocial and contextual factors shaping ACP engagement;(3)Patient values and communication in ACP decision-making; and (4) Strategies and support for ACP delivery.limited patient and caregiver awareness, emotional strain, family disagreement, and differing views on the timing of ACP discussions as important implementation challenges. Participants emphasized the need for professional guidance and communication tailored to patients and caregivers. Healthcare professionals also emphasized the importance of enhanced training, adequate staffing, standardized procedures, policy support, and support from artificial intelligence. Conclusions ACP engagement was limited among the patients interviewed.patients and healthcare professionals also differed in their views on the timing of ACP discussions. Professional guidance and communication between patients and their families, as well as training and support for medical staff may facilitate the implementation of ACP.

Single-cell technologies, coupled with powerful machine learning, have multiplied the number of named innate immune cell states faster than their biological features have been established. Innate cell identity is generated by at least four partially independent axes (ontogeny, maturation, response to microbial or damage signals, and tissue adaptation) that project onto a shared transcriptional space. Consequently, snapshot expression data alone cannot uniquely attribute an observed partition to any one of these processes. Data-driven taxonomy has been particularly effective where one axis provides a stable interpretative anchor, as in ontogeny-defined conventional dendritic cells, and faces greater challenges where several axes interact, as in granulocytes, tissue-adapted macrophages, and ILCs. Here, we assess what recent atlas and foundation model studies have resolved, identify independent biological validation rather than computational resolution as the current bottleneck, and propose an explicit evidence hierarchy for deciding when computational clusters should be considered bona fide biological entities.

Forage production currently faces multifaceted pressures, including resource constraints, climate fluctuations, and escalating labour costs. Accurately and promptly acquiring data on forage growth status and translating it into operational prescriptions is crucial for enhancing forage utilisation efficiency and production sustainability. This paper presents a comprehensive review of intelligent forage production, focusing on multi-source perception, biomass and yield estimation, precision operations, and system synergy. To ensure a rigorous synthesis, a structured literature search was conducted across Web of Science, Scopus, and CNKI, covering publications up to August 2026. Firstly, the roles of ground-based, near-surface, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellite platforms in monitoring plant height, canopy structure, spectral characteristics, moisture, and nutrients are compared; this is then followed by an analysis of data acquisition and calibration methods across varying spatial scales and temporal resolutions. Secondly, strategies for biomass and quality estimation—based on vegetation indices, red-edge and short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectroscopy, canopy height and three-dimensional (3D) structure, as well as machine learning—are synthesised. Particular emphasis is placed on the impacts of soil background, spectral saturation, mixed-sward heterogeneity, post-mowing regeneration, and cross-regional generalisation on model accuracy. Furthermore, precision operation technologies, such as variable-rate irrigation, fertilisation, optimal harvest window identification, cutting control, baling, and autonomous navigation, are summarised. The prerequisites for synergy among perception, estimation, decision-making, execution, and operational feedback are also analysed. A key synthesized finding is that structural-spectral feature fusion only yields actionable precision gains when temporal synchronization and spatial scale matching are strictly enforced, and continuous simplified local calibration remains indispensable for cross-regional model generalization. Finally, the integration of open-access multi-source data, the fusion of physical models with artificial intelligence (AI), rigorous external validation, and farmer-oriented low-cost deployment are proposed as key priorities for future research.

Environmental chemical exposure has emerged as an important contributor to cardiovascular disease. Despite the exponential increase in the number of chemicals detected in environmental and human samples, cardiovascular toxicity data remain scarce for the vast majority of these compounds. The intricate architecture of the cardiovascular system yields complex and heterogeneous responses to chemical exposure, whereas conventional cardiovascular toxicity testing approaches are plagued by critical drawbacks, including limited phenotypic end points, poor mechanistic implication, inadequate efficacy and accuracy, and a lack of dynamic functional readouts. To address these gaps, we introduce the concept of the cardiovascular toxicity phenome (CTP) characterized by the totality of observable cardiovascular characteristics or traits encompassing cellular morphology, tissue architecture, and functional performance, induced by hazardous chemical exposures. To facilitate efficient quantification of the complex phenotypic indicators derived from the CTP, we propose an integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-aided testing platforms to analyze multiscale data sets generated from cell-, tissue-, and organ-level observations, thereby delineating the hierarchical organization of the vascular network and dynamic patterns within the cardiovascular system. This emerging paradigm remedies the shortcomings of traditional assays and establishes a framework for new approach methodologies (NAMs) in bolstering the cardiovascular toxicity assessment of environmental chemicals.

Oral diseases remain a public health challenge worldwide and disproportionately affect populations with limited access to prevention and care. In Shenzhen, rapid urbanisation, internal migration, and social diversity may contribute to heterogeneity in oral disease risk, preventive behaviours, and service utilisation, highlighting the need for prevention-oriented policies. To address this need, a multidisciplinary forum was convened in Shenzhen on 20 November 2025, bringing together academics, health policymakers, epidemiologists, and oral health professionals. Before the forum, background materials on local epidemiological data and published evidence were circulated. During the forum, participants deliberated on these materials and reached broad agreement on strategic priorities, which were then synthesised into a four-pillar framework. The aim of this article is to present this expert-informed framework and to describe its rationale and policy implications for Shenzhen. The first pillar focuses on governance and infrastructure, including the establishment of an Oral Health Prevention Collaborative Network to improve coordination across schools, community services, public health, and clinical care. The second pillar emphasises workforce development and public mobilisation through training for primary care and community-based personnel, as well as population-level health promotion. The third pillar addresses technology and evidence-based interventions, such as teledentistry, artificial intelligence-assisted screening, caries prevention with fluoride varnish. The fourth pillar promotes integration into universal health coverage by expanding coverage for preventive and essential dental services and reducing out-of-pocket costs for vulnerable groups. Together, these pillars provide a preliminary expert-informed blueprint for improving oral health equity in Shenzhen. The framework aligns with global priorities in prevention, primary care integration, and financial protection, and may provide a basis for further discussion in other rapidly developing urban settings, subject to local adaptation and evaluation.

Background/Objectives: Healthcare AI systems described as agentic may improve selected tasks, but gains can reflect models, information access, human support or complete intervention packages. We mapped clinical utility, safety and workflow consequences while distinguishing functional agency from evidence isolating its contribution. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searches, through 11 September 2026. Eligible evidence comprised original empirical journal reports of healthcare systems described as agentic or demonstrating potentially agentic functions. Two authors independently screened records, and two independently extracted data, with adjudication. All four authors jointly assigned analytical classifications after a five-report pilot. A structured critical audit and descriptive Clinical Agency Evidence Chain informed synthesis. The review was not registered. Results: The corpus included 123 reports; 90 were classified as core or bounded functionally agentic. Within this subset, technical task performance was the endpoint category in 44/90 reports (48.9%), and clinical decision/process outcomes in 33/90 (36.7%). Three randomised reports in the broader corpus assessed patient health outcomes: one core, one boundary/non-agentic and one indeterminate. All evaluated bundled interventions. Evidence isolating agency and following its consequences within the same comparison was limited. Safety ascertainment, intended-user error correction and whole-pathway workload were incompletely reported. External or temporal validation occurred in 6/90 reports (6.7%), with partial validation in seven others. Predominantly retrospective, simulated or offline evidence limited clinical inference. Conclusions: Intervention-level benefit must be distinguished from the incremental contribution of agency. Technical gains and local or estimated time savings do not establish patient benefit or reduced total human work. Mechanistic comparisons and prospective clinical evaluations address complementary questions. Adoption decisions should consider benefits, harms, implementation conditions and uncertainty.

documents.abstract: This research paper presents the design and development of an AI-based personal productivity assistant aimed at improving task management, time organisation, scheduling, and productivity tracking. The proposed system provides a unified platform where users can manage daily tasks, set priorities and deadlines, schedule activities, receive reminders, and monitor task completion. The current prototype is being developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to provide a simple, accessible, and user-friendly interface. The paper discusses the problem of managing multiple responsibilities, existing approaches to digital productivity assistance, the proposed system architecture, development methodology, implementation status, and future enhancements. It also explores the potential integration of intelligent task prioritisation, adaptive scheduling, and personalised recommendations. The project aims to provide a foundation for a smarter productivity management system that can help students and working professionals organise their daily activities more effectively. As the current prototype is partially developed, further implementation and testing are required to evaluate its effectiveness.

documents.abstract: This paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence into the manufacturing sector, focusing on its applications in process optimization, product design, and sustainability, with a particular case study on cream cheese production within the Greek food and beverage industry. Four main types of AI technologies—a.) Data Analysis, b.) Machine and Deep Learning, c.) Optimization Algorithms, and d.) Generative Models—are discussed in the context of their roles in manufacturing. These are applied to five major areas within the manufacturing industry: 1.) Design and Engineering, 2.) Process Monitoring and Control, 3.) Manufacturing Operations, 4.) Production Chain, and 5.) Supply Chain. A detailed case study is presented, which demonstrates the application of AI in optimizing the production process of cream cheese, aiming to reduce resource consumption and improve production efficiency. The results indicate a notable improvement in sustainability metrics, particularly in energy and water usage, while maintaining consistent product quality. This work demonstrates the transformative potential of AI in enhancing both operational efficiency and environmental sustainability in manufacturing processes.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a corporate communicator and examines how AI source transparency influences message credibility, employee trust, employee engagement and ultimately brand advocacy. Specifically, the study explores both cognition-based and affect-based dimensions of trust and evaluates the moderating role of AI literacy in shaping employees’ responses to AI-generated communication. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted using an online survey questionnaire. Data were collected from 317 employees across different organizations who had experience with AI-mediated communication in their workplace. Structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.0 was applied to test the proposed relationships and evaluate the conceptual framework. Findings The findings indicate that AI source transparency positively affects message credibility. Message credibility significantly enhances both cognition-based and affect-based trust, which subsequently increase employee engagement. Employee engagement was also found to positively influence brand advocacy. However, AI literacy showed an unexpected negative moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and cognition-based trust, suggesting that employees with greater AI knowledge become more critical and skeptical of AI-generated content, whereas its moderating effect on the relationship between message credibility and affect-based trust is not statistically significant. Practical implications Organizations should not use AI solely as an automation tool but also as a strategic communication instrument. Transparency regarding AI usage, combined with human oversight and quality assurance mechanisms, can strengthen credibility and trust. Companies should also invest in content governance and monitoring practices to ensure that AI-generated communication remains accurate, relevant, and aligned with organizational values. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-mediated corporate communication by developing and empirically testing an integrated model linking AI transparency, message credibility, trust, engagement and brand advocacy. It also provides novel insights into the complex role of AI literacy in influencing employee perceptions and trust toward AI-generated communication.

documents.abstract: Access to legal information in Saudi Arabia remains challenging despite the public availability of its laws, particularly in commercial disputes where relevant provisions are distributed across multiple legal frameworks and expressed in formal language that can be difficult for non-specialists to interpret. This paper presents an AI-powered legal advisory system for Saudi commercial cases that uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide legal guidance grounded directly in statutory text. Given a complaint written in natural Arabic, the system identifies the relevant Saudi laws, retrieves the applicable legal articles, and generates a structured legal opinion covering an analysis of the case, a direct answer to the user’s question, the supporting legal provisions, the user’s rights, and an assessment of the strength of the user’s legal position. Unlike general-purpose legal assistants, the system does not rely on unsupported legal knowledge or attempt to predict judicial outcomes; its substantive claims are grounded in retrieved legal provisions. The system was evaluated on 200 real commercial cases from the Saudi Ministry of Justice judicial portal, for which actual court rulings and judge-cited articles were available as references. Three independent large language models—Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek, and GPT-4o—were tested as candidate generation models, achieving overall scores of 76.0%, 81.9%, and 87.0%, respectively. GPT-4o was selected as the primary generation model following this benchmark evaluation using different metrics such as retrieval coverage, article coverage, ruling accuracy, legal justification, and completeness. The results demonstrate the potential of retrieval-based legal systems to provide traceable and accessible legal guidance for Arabic-speaking users in the Saudi commercial law domain. The proposed solution has also been integrated into a live application, demonstrating its practical applicability and potential to provide accessible legal guidance to the general public.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping academic learning by enabling students to delegate cognitively demanding tasks, raising questions about the preservation of student agency and independent learning capacities within sustainable higher education. This study examines whether AI literacy is associated with learning autonomy primarily through critical AI evaluation, responsible AI use, and cognitive offloading rather than through a direct relationship alone. Survey data from 2111 university students in Serbia, the United Kingdom, and Germany were analyzed using structural equation modeling, serial mediation, and multi-group comparisons. AI literacy was positively associated with critical AI evaluation, which was positively related to responsible AI use. Responsible AI use was positively associated with learning autonomy and negatively associated with cognitive offloading, while cognitive offloading was negatively related to learning autonomy. Both serial indirect pathways were significant, whereas the direct association between AI literacy and learning autonomy was nonsignificant. No statistically significant differences in the examined relationships were detected across the three national samples. The findings extend research on sustainable AI-supported higher education by distinguishing technological competence from the evaluative and behavioral practices associated with student agency. They highlight cognitive delegation as an important dimension of the relationship between GenAI engagement and self-reported learning autonomy, offering insights into educational practices that seek to integrate technological assistance while supporting independent reasoning.

Artificial intelligence is embedded in translation learning and professional workflows, yet translator education lacks an integrated evidence-based account of the knowledge, judgement, assessment, and professional responsibility needed for accountable AI-assisted translation. This study conducted a qualitative evidence synthesis of empirical research on AI literacy in translator education, using systematic searches of Scopus and Web of Science supplemented by citation tracking and manual searching. Professional-practice studies were coded separately to contextualise workplace responsibilities and conditions rather than to provide evidence of classroom effectiveness. The final corpus comprised 22 studies, including 18 core translator-education studies and four professional-practice studies. The synthesis identifies critical translation judgement as the organising capability of translation-specific AI literacy and integrates five dimensions across four curriculum-design domains: conceptual and technical foundations, situated pedagogical practice, assessment for accountable use, and ethical-professional positioning. The framework identifies equitable access and scaffolding, educator expertise, curriculum coordination, infrastructure, authentic project opportunities, and assessment capacity as cross-cutting implementation conditions. The findings support a shift from tool-centred AI literacy towards students’ ability to evaluate, verify, revise, reject, and justify AI-supported translation decisions while retaining responsibility for the final product. The evidence base is heterogeneous, limited to English-language publications, and geographically concentrated in East Asia, particularly China. This study synthesizes empirical research on AI literacy in translator education to establish an evidence-informed curriculum-design framework centered on critical translation judgment. By synthesizing 22 key studies across educational and professional contexts, the work provides educators and curriculum designers with a structured heuristic covering foundational knowledge, pedagogical practices, assessment, and professional ethics. Its significance lies in guiding a paradigm shift from tool-centered technical instruction toward fostering students' capacity to critically evaluate, verify, and justify AI-assisted translation outputs while maintaining accountability for the final text.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming higher education by influencing teaching, learning, assessment, research, academic administration, and student support. In India, this transformation has gained particular significance following the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasises technology-enabled education, multidisciplinary learning, creativity, critical thinking, skill development, and preparation for an evolving knowledge economy. The emerging concept of Education 5.0 further emphasises human-centred, ethical, sustainable, and collaborative relationships between people and intelligent technologies. However, successful AI integration in Indian higher education depends not only on technological availability but also on AI readiness, technology acceptance, digital pedagogical competence, self-regulated learning, institutional support, and ethical awareness. This study examines the relationships among AI readiness, AI acceptance, AI-supported digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and learner engagement within the context of Indian higher education. A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected through validated questionnaires from 250 higher-education teachers and students, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with 20 participants. Quantitative data were examined using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis, while qualitative data were analysed through thematic analysis. The findings indicate positive relationships among AI readiness, AI acceptance, digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and learner engagement. The qualitative findings highlight the potential of AI for personalised learning, feedback, academic support, and independent learning while also identifying concerns related to academic integrity, data privacy, misinformation, overdependence, unequal access, and institutional preparedness. The study proposes an India-sensitive framework in which AI readiness functions as a foundation for responsible AI acceptance and pedagogical transformation. The paper concludes that advancing Education 5.0 in Indian higher education requires coordinated investment in AI literacy, faculty development, digital infrastructure, ethical governance, inclusive access, curriculum transformation, and human-centred pedagogical innovation.

documents.abstract: Can firms in developing economies translate readiness for artificial intelligence (AI) into higher productivity and greater AI adoption? This paper develops Firm-Level AI Enablement Index (FAEI), a composite measure of Power Reliability, Digital Connectivity, Human Capital, and Institutional Environment. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data for 44,251 firms across 76 low- and middle-income economies and a 2026 follow-up covering 3,579 firms in seven economies, the analysis examines the relationship between readiness, adoption, and productivity. The findings are as follows. First, the FAEI is strongly associated with labour productivity. A 0.1 increase in FAEI is associated with 11.5 percent higher sales per worker, conditional on country, sector, and survey-year fixed effects. Second, Human Capital shows the strongest positive association among the four pillars, followed by Power Reliability and Digital Connectivity. Third, FAEI is not consistently associated with AI adoption. However, firm-level digital practices, particularly website presence and electronic payments, are positively associated with AI adoption and several measures of AI engagement. Fourth, AI adoption is not significantly associated with productivity in the 2026 follow-up and readiness is no more strongly associated with productivity in industries with greater AI exposure. These findings highlight the heterogeneity between the capabilities associated with firm productivity and practices associated with AI adoption. For developing economies, strengthening Human Capital and foundational digital capabilities may be important priorities for improving firm performance and supporting AI adoption.

documents.abstract: Curriculum mapping is essential for competency-based dental education but is often time-consuming and dependent on faculty interpretation. As dental schools undergo digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools may enhance curriculum quality assurance and alignment processes. Large language models (LLMs) may support curriculum alignment tasks; however, evidence in dental education remains limited. This study compared the accuracy, quality, efficiency, and faculty acceptance of ChatGPT-assisted versus manual curriculum mapping. A fixed-order, repeated-measures comparative study included 90 dental faculty members from Periodontology, Oral Medicine, and Oral Diagnosis. Participants completed manual mapping followed by ChatGPT-assisted mapping after a seven-day washout period, aligning course-level Intended Learning Outcomes with Program Learning Outcomes. Mapping accuracy against an independent, Delphi-derived reference standard was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included rubric-based mapping quality, task completion time, error patterns, and faculty perceptions assessed using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The primary comparison used participant-level paired t-tests, with participant-clustered logistic generalized estimating equations used to assess incorrect mapping occurrence. Mapping accuracy was significantly higher with ChatGPT assistance than with manual mapping (78.8% ± 7.9% vs. 74.3% ± 8.2%; mean difference = 4.5% points, 95% CI 2.81–6.19; Cohen’s d_z = 0.56; p < 0.001). A secondary participant-clustered analysis supported this finding, showing lower odds of incorrect mapping (OR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.62–0.98; p = 0.035). ChatGPT-assisted mapping yielded higher rubric-based quality scores (25.67 ± 0.26 vs. 20.96 ± 0.36; p < 0.001) and shorter completion times (14.0 ± 1.5 vs. 27.8 ± 2.9 min; p < 0.001). The participant-clustered analysis found no statistically significant difference in the relative distribution of error types between methods ( p = 0.053). Faculty reported favorable technology acceptance, with all three TAM constructs rated significantly above the neutral midpoint (all p < 0.001). ChatGPT-assisted mapping was associated with significantly higher mapping accuracy, higher rubric-based quality scores, and shorter completion times than manual mapping. However, the fixed-order, non-randomized design precludes attributing these differences exclusively to AI assistance, as practice and familiarity effects may have contributed to the observed results. These findings support further evaluation of LLMs as faculty-supervised decision-support tools for curriculum alignment, particularly through randomized, counterbalanced, multicenter studies.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can improve students’ work, but an AI-assisted answer does not show whether they can reason alone. This quasi-experiment examined whether tax reasoning demonstrated with AI assistance was maintained when 41 Business Administration students reconstructed it independently. In a digital economy taxation case, the experimental group (n = 20) used the TaxDigital Tutor, an AI tutor developed for this study that guides reasoning without supplying answers, whereas the control group (n = 21) could use generative AI and other resources. All students immediately reconstructed their reasoning by hand without assistance, and both phases were scored with the same five-criterion rubric. Overall, scores were 14.3 points lower in the unassisted reconstruction (F(1, 39) = 18.39, p < 0.001). Scores declined by 17.9 points in the control group (p < 0.001) and by 10.6 points in the experimental group (p = 0.060); however, the exploratory between-group comparison was not significant (p = 0.282). Using case data as evidence was the lowest-scoring criterion in both phases. These findings suggest that scores obtained with AI do not necessarily reflect performance without it. The study also proposes the From Assisted to Autonomous (A2A) framework for progressively reducing AI assistance and assessing independent performance.

documents.abstract: Background Voice-based artificial intelligence may offer a noninvasive approach to identifying patients at elevated risk for laryngeal cancer, but successful implementation depends on its acceptability and fit within primary care. This study examined primary care clinicians’ approaches to persistent dysphonia, perceptions of artificial intelligence–assisted voice-based risk stratification, and factors influencing clinical implementation. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional mixed-methods study using semi-structured interviews and an anonymous electronic survey that could be completed independently. Interviews explored dysphonia evaluation, referral practices, technology use, and perceived implementation considerations. Survey items assessed clinical reasoning using two dysphonia vignettes, technology readiness, application acceptability, and perceived barriers. Survey responses were summarized using descriptive statistics; no inferential statistical testing was performed. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, and qualitative and quantitative findings were subsequently integrated at the aggregate level. Results Fifteen clinicians participated in interviews, and 16 anonymous survey responses were received. In a clinical vignette of a patient with a smoking history who presented for persistent dysphonia, all respondents identified laryngeal or other head and neck malignancy in the differential diagnosis, compared with 12 of 15 (80.0%) for a similar clinical vignette without a smoking history. Thirteen of 16 survey respondents (81.3%) reported a positive or very positive initial impression of the proposed application, and 11 (68.8%) were comfortable or very comfortable integrating it into clinical practice. Interviews revealed that clinicians generally lacked a standardized pathway for escalating persistent dysphonia and viewed artificial intelligence primarily as decision support rather than a replacement for clinical judgment. Acceptance was conditional on demonstrated accuracy, minimal workflow disruption, appropriate clinician oversight, efficient referral pathways, and attention to equity, privacy, and accountability. Conclusions Primary care clinicians demonstrated interest in voice-based artificial intelligence for laryngeal cancer risk stratification, but willingness to adopt the technology depended on more than diagnostic performance. Successful implementation will require integration into existing workflows, preservation of clinical oversight, clear pathways from risk identification to definitive evaluation, and attention to patient trust and equitable access.

documents.abstract: Misleading news often reaches readers before its claims can be checked, which has encouraged research into artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) as tools for flagging content that needs closer examination. This paper reviews 31 publications from 2011 to 2024 and organises their approaches into four groups: traditional machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based models, and multi-source or real-time systems. It then tests one concern that recurs in the literature, namely that scores measured on one dataset do not carry over to another. Four standard classifiers (Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, and Random Forest, all on TF-IDF features) were evaluated on two public datasets: Fake or Real News (2016 political articles) and CoAID (2020 COVID-19 articles). Within Fake or Real News, five-fold macro-F1 ranges from 0.87 to 0.94. When a model trained on one dataset is tested on the other, macro-F1 falls to between 0.06 and 0.42. A model trained on an early CoAID snapshot also detects few fake articles in later snapshots, although the later test set holds only 15 fake articles, so that result is inconclusive. The highest-weighted terms of the linear models include source and formatting words, which suggests dataset-specific shortcuts. The paper also specifies CAMMS, a multilingual and multimodal framework with an explanation layer. CAMMS is described and given an evaluation plan, but it has not been implemented or evaluated here. The review finds no basis for naming one model family as best in every setting, and it points to cross-dataset testing, multilingual evaluation, transparent reporting, and human oversight as priorities.

—Gas leakage, fire incidents, and abnormal envi- ronmental conditions create safety risks in homes, laborato- ries, workshops, and industrial settings. This paper presents RiskSense, an ESP32-based Internet of Things (IoT) prototype designed to monitor gas-sensitive readings, flame status, tempera- ture, and humidity. The prototype combines an MQ-2 gas sensor, a digital flame sensor, and a DHT11 sensor with local indicators, a buzzer, a motor driver, and the Blynk IoT platform. Sensor readings are processed using configurable thresholdbased logic for local alarms, while status values and alerts can be viewed remotely through a Wi-Fi-connected dashboard. An artificial intelligence (AI) layer based on a Random Forest classifier is implemented to classify the monitored conditions into NORMAL, WARNING, and CRITICAL risk categories. Isolation Forest for unusual sensor-pattern detection is proposed as future work. The paper describes the system architecture, hardware and software design, control logic, the Random Forest algorithm used, implementation methodology, validation plan, limitations, and future work. Since measured experimental results and numerical model-evaluation metrics have not been provided, no numerical performance claims are made. Index Terms—Internet of Things, ESP32, MQ-2, flame detec- tion, DHT11, gas leakage, fire detection, environmental monitor- ing, Blynk, Random Forest, machine learning.

This research paper presents CivicWeave, an AI-based predictive civic grievance intelligence system designed to improve the identification, analysis, and prioritization of civic complaints. The proposed system analyzes civic complaints using their textual content, geographical locations, and submission timestamps to identify potentially related reports. It aims to help municipal authorities recognize recurring civic issues, understand complaint patterns, and identify incidents that may require greater attention. CivicWeave considers factors such as semantic similarity, geographical proximity, temporal information, complaint frequency, distinct citizen participation, citizen support, unresolved duration, and safety-related keywords to support incident analysis and priority assessment. It also incorporates a human-review mechanism through which municipal officers can review, approve, or reject suggested complaint relationships. The system is developed using React for the frontend, FastAPI for backend services, and MongoDB for data storage. It also supports optional Gemini-based text embeddings with a deterministic local fallback mechanism. The research focuses on improving civic grievance management through AI-assisted complaint analysis, incident identification, explainable prioritization, and human-centered decision-making. documents.abstract: This narrative review examines where artificial intelligence (AI) improves aquaculture environmental monitoring relative to conventional methods, how validation designs shape the interpretation of reported gains, and what evidence is needed for routine farm use. A thematic synthesis, supplemented by a targeted OpenAlex literature update, compares baselines, validation designs, and measured outcomes across water-quality monitoring, harmful algal bloom surveillance, contaminant sensing, and environmental management. In a flow-through farm, a neural time-series model improved imputation of influent dissolved oxygen (DO), while linear interpolation performed best for tank DO. In a separate six-pond evaluation within one farm, physics-guided transfer learning reduced the mean absolute error of nighttime DO forecasts by 35.5% relative to a standard long short-term memory model. In a 45-day pilot in one koi pond, integrated predictive control used 26.86% less energy than manual operation. These findings support task-specific use of AI for monitoring and decision support. Broader deployment of automated control requires independent farm validation and prospective assessment of water quality and resource use.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly optimising pharmaceutical formulation by enabling more precise, faster and cost-efficient drug formulation processes. Integration of AI technologies (such as machine learning and deep learning) with pharmaceutical formulation is commonly applied in drug formulation, including artificial neural networks (ANN) and logic systems. The integration of AI with formulation can predict drug behaviour, select excipients for optimisation, and design safer and more efficient dosage forms compared to traditional methods. AI-enabled instruments are currently employed across the pharmaceutical industry, in areas such as formulation optimisation, QC, and stability testing. Adoption of AI results in improved efficiency with data-driven decision-making and the ability to handle complex, multi-variable formulation problems; on the other hand, notable disadvantages such as high implementation costs, dependency on quality data, regulatory challenges, and the need for specialised technical expertise are observed. AI in pharmaceutical formulation has a wide scope in future, as it has the potential to revolutionise the production of medicine, accelerate novel drug delivery system design, and regulatory compliance processes. As AI continues to evolve, its role in pharmaceutical sciences is expected to expand significantly, bridging the gap between computational innovation and practical drug manufacturing, ultimately contributing to safer, more effective, and more accessible pharmaceutical products. This study comprises a detailed review of the application of artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical formulations, including the integration of existing technology with artificial intelligence.
